title: Frozen Shoulder Causes, Stages and Recovery: A Physiotherapist’s Guide
summary: Learn frozen shoulder causes, symptoms, stages and recovery, plus safe exercises and physio care in Bengaluru.

sections.content: Can’t fasten a seatbelt, comb your hair or reach a high shelf without a deep, nagging ache? A shoulder that gets steadily stiffer and sorer over weeks is often more than a muscle strain. It could be frozen shoulder.

Frozen shoulder, medically known as adhesive capsulitis, affects the capsule, the thin layer of connective tissue wrapped around the shoulder joint. The capsule becomes inflamed, thickened and tight, so the joint gradually loses movement and can feel locked in place.

It is most common in adults between 40-60 and affects women more often than men. Recovery is slow, usually many months and sometimes two to three years, but most people do improve, and the right care at the right stage makes the journey far more comfortable. This guide covers frozen shoulder causes, symptoms, stages, treatment and safe exercises, along with when to get assessed.

In short: frozen shoulder is a stiff, painful shoulder that moves through freezing, frozen and thawing stages. It is more likely with diabetes or thyroid problems, and it is diagnosed by examining how your shoulder moves. Gentle, stage-matched exercise and physiotherapy help, and most people regain good function over time.
What Causes Frozen Shoulder?

In many people there is no clear trigger. This is called primary frozen shoulder: the capsule becomes inflamed, then scars and tightens, leaving the joint less room to move. Why this starts is still not fully understood.
It is not caused by one bad movement, and it is not simply a sign of overuse or a weak shoulder.
Secondary frozen shoulder follows something identifiable, such as an injury, surgery or another health condition. The main risk factors are:

items: Diabetes: People with diabetes are several times more likely to develop frozen shoulder and it often lasts longer. Changes in connective tissue are thought to play a part. This is worth knowing in India, where diabetes is common.
Thyroid disorders: Both an underactive and an overactive thyroid are linked with a higher risk.
Injury or surgery: Fractures, dislocations and shoulder or upper-limb surgery can set the stage, particularly when movement is restricted afterwards.
Prolonged immobility: A sling worn longer than needed, or avoiding the arm because it hurts, lets the capsule stiffen. This is why gentle early movement matters once your clinician says it is safe.
Age and sex: Risk is highest between 40 and 60, and women are affected more often.
Other conditions: Heart disease and Parkinson’s disease have also been linked with frozen shoulder.

sections.content: Symptoms: How to Spot Frozen Shoulder Early
Symptoms build gradually. The first sign is often a deep ache in the outer shoulder or upper arm that is worse at night. Common symptoms include:

items: Persistent shoulder pain that can spread into the upper arm.
Night pain, especially when lying on the affected side.
Increasing stiffness when reaching overhead, behind your back or across your body.
Difficulty with everyday tasks such as dressing, combing your hair or driving.

sections.content: The hallmark of frozen shoulder is loss of external rotation, which means turning your arm outwards with the elbow tucked into your side. Movement is limited whether you lift the arm yourself or someone else moves it for you. That is what separates it from a rotator cuff problem, where the arm is weak but can usually still be moved passively through full range.
Is It Really Frozen Shoulder?

Diagnosis is mostly clinical. A physiotherapist or doctor tests your active and passive movement and asks about your history, including diabetes and thyroid problems. X-ray or ultrasound is sometimes used to rule out arthritis, calcific tendinitis or a rotator cuff tear. Neck problems can also refer pain into the shoulder, so the neck is checked as well. Getting the diagnosis right matters, because exercises that help frozen shoulder can aggravate other shoulder problems.
The Three Stages of Frozen Shoulder
Frozen shoulder usually moves through three overlapping stages: freezing, frozen and thawing. Timelines are approximate and differ from person to person.
Stage 1: Freezing (about 6 weeks to 9 months)

This is usually the most painful phase. Pain builds, especially at night and with overhead movement, and the shoulder starts to stiffen. Treatment focuses on settling pain and keeping comfortable movement, with gentle, pain-guided exercises. Aggressive stretching can make this stage worse.
Stage 2: Frozen (about 4 to 12 months)

Pain often eases, but stiffness takes over. The capsule is tight in every direction, so lifting, rotating and reaching behind you are all restricted. Physiotherapy shifts towards mobility: joint mobilisation, controlled stretching and graded movement, with intensity matched to how irritable the shoulder is.
Stage 3: Thawing (about 6 months to 2 years or longer)

Movement gradually returns and everyday tasks become easier. Treatment now rebuilds flexibility, strength and confidence so the shoulder works properly again. Strengthening the shoulder blade and rotator cuff muscles usually begins here.
How Long Does Frozen Shoulder Recovery Take?

Overall, frozen shoulder can take several months to two or three years to resolve. Severity, stage, underlying conditions such as diabetes and how you respond to treatment all affect the timeline. Some people have mild stiffness even after pain settles. Rather than watching the calendar, track function: dressing without pain, reaching a shelf, sleeping through the night.
Progress is rarely a straight line, and a sore week does not mean you are back at the start.
Frozen Shoulder Treatment Options
Treatment aims to reduce pain, restore movement and return you to daily activity. The right approach depends on your stage and symptoms.
Physiotherapy for Frozen Shoulder
A physiotherapist assesses your range of movement, pain levels and daily limitations, then builds a plan that may include:

items: Gentle mobility exercises.
Controlled stretching.
Joint mobilisation.
Progressive strengthening.
Advice on sleeping positions and everyday tasks, such as supporting the arm on a pillow at night.

sections.content: The guiding rule is simple: be gentle when the shoulder is painful, and progress when stiffness is the main problem. Consistency beats intensity.
At a first visit, expect questions about your pain, sleep and daily tasks, a hands-on movement check of both shoulders and a clear plan with realistic timelines.
Medication and Medical Interventions

A doctor may suggest pain relief or anti-inflammatory medicines. A corticosteroid injection can calm pain, particularly in the early stages. Hydrodilatation, where fluid is injected to stretch the capsule, may be considered in some cases. Surgery, such as manipulation under anaesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release, is reserved for people whose symptoms stay severe despite months of non-surgical care. Always make these decisions with a qualified doctor.
Exercises That May Help Frozen Shoulder

Movement helps, but timing matters. Move into a gentle stretch, not sharp pain, and keep sessions short and frequent. Warm the shoulder first, move slowly and breathe normally. Any soreness should settle within about an hour. If it does not, you have done too much.
Freezing stage (painful)

items: Pendulum swings: Lean forward with your good hand on a table and let the affected arm hang. Sway it gently forwards, backwards and in small circles for one to two minutes, a few times a day.
Shoulder blade squeezes: Draw your shoulder blades together, hold for five seconds and relax. Repeat 10 times.

sections.content: Frozen stage (stiff)

items: Wall walks: Face a wall and slowly walk your fingers upwards as far as is comfortable. Repeat 10 times, two to three times a day.
Assisted external rotation: With your elbow tucked in, hold a stick and use your good arm to guide the affected hand outwards. Hold for 10 seconds and repeat 10 times.

sections.content: Thawing stage (regaining range)

items: Towel stretch: Hold a towel behind your back with your good arm above and the affected arm below. Gently pull upwards with the good arm and hold for 10 seconds. Repeat 5 times.

sections.content: These are examples, not a prescription. A physiotherapist can tell you which ones suit your stage.
What Should You Avoid If You Have Frozen Shoulder?
Certain habits can slow recovery. Try to avoid:

items: Forcing the shoulder through painful movements.
Aggressive stretching during the painful stage.
Keeping the shoulder completely still for long periods.
Lifting heavy objects overhead if they flare symptoms.
Following random exercise routines without knowing your limits.
Ignoring persistent pain and increasing stiffness.

sections.content: Complete rest is generally not recommended unless your clinician advises it. The goal is comfortable movement without irritating the shoulder further.
Easing Everyday Life With a Frozen Shoulder

Small changes make daily life easier while the shoulder recovers. Sleep on your back or on the unaffected side, with a pillow supporting the sore arm. A warm shower or heat pack before exercises can loosen the shoulder. Dress the affected arm first and undress it last, keep frequently used items between waist and chest height, and break overhead tasks into short bursts. Keep using the arm within your comfort range, because gentle everyday movement is part of recovery.
Can Frozen Shoulder Be Prevented?

There is no guaranteed way to prevent it, especially when it appears without a clear cause. Keeping the shoulder moving after an injury or surgery, once your clinician says it is safe, may reduce the risk linked to prolonged immobility. Managing diabetes and thyroid conditions under medical supervision also helps. Regular movement also supports your joint health. If you notice persistent pain or growing stiffness, get advice early rather than waiting for it to worsen.
When Should You See a Physiotherapist?

Consider an assessment if shoulder pain lasts several weeks, movement is becoming restricted, night pain disturbs your sleep or everyday tasks are getting harder. Early assessment confirms whether it is frozen shoulder or something else, and helps you avoid exercises that aggravate it. Do not wait for it to thaw on its own if sleep, work or daily tasks are already affected.
Seek urgent medical attention for sudden severe pain after an injury, visible deformity, sudden weakness, or shoulder discomfort with chest pain.
Get Your Shoulder Moving Again in Bangalore

Frozen shoulder is slow, but it is rarely permanent, and the right plan changes how it feels along the way. Whether your shoulder is just starting to ache or has been stiff for months, a stage-based plan can save you weeks of guesswork. Book an assessment to find out where your shoulder is in its recovery.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the main cause of frozen shoulder?

Inflammation and thickening of the capsule around the shoulder joint. Often there is no clear trigger, but diabetes, thyroid disorders, injury, surgery and prolonged immobilisation are recognised risk factors.
How long does frozen shoulder take to heal?
Anywhere from several months to two or three years, depending on severity, stage, underlying conditions and response to treatment.
Can physiotherapy help with frozen shoulder?
Yes. Physiotherapy can help manage pain, improve mobility and restore strength through stage-appropriate exercises, stretching and mobilisation.
Is it safe to exercise with frozen shoulder?
Yes, if the exercises suit your stage. Choose gentle movements when pain is high, avoid aggressive stretching and ask a physiotherapist for guidance.
Can frozen shoulder happen again?
Recurrence in the same shoulder is uncommon, but some people develop it in the opposite shoulder, particularly when risk factors such as diabetes are present.
Does frozen shoulder go away on its own?

In most people it gradually improves over time, but this can take a long while and some stiffness may linger. Treatment will not rush the stages, but it can ease pain, protect movement and keep you functioning while the shoulder recovers.
What is the best sleeping position with frozen shoulder?
Lying on your back, or on the unaffected side, with a pillow supporting the sore arm is usually most comfortable. Avoid lying on the affected shoulder, especially in the painful freezing stage.
How is frozen shoulder different from a rotator cuff injury?

In frozen shoulder, the joint is stiff whether you move it or someone else does, and turning the arm outwards is especially limited. With a rotator cuff problem, the arm is usually weak but can often still be moved passively through full range.

title: ACL Rehab: What to Expect at Every Stage of Recovery
summary: A torn ACL is one of the most feared injuries in sport — but with the right protocol, a full return is not just possible, it's the norm. Here's what your recovery timeline actually looks like.

sections.content: An ACL rupture brings your training to a full stop, but it doesn't have to end your sporting life. At Stance, we've guided hundreds of athletes through reconstruction and back to competitive sport — and the single biggest factor in outcome quality is the quality of the rehabilitation protocol.
Phase 1 — Weeks 0–6: Protecting the Graft

Immediately after surgery, the priority is protecting the new graft while managing swelling and beginning to restore range of motion. You'll work on quad activation, straight-leg raises, and gentle knee flexion. Full weight-bearing in an extension brace is typically introduced within the first week.
Ice, elevation, and compression in the first 72 hours significantly reduce effusion and allow faster progression into active rehab.
Phase 2 — Weeks 6–12: Rebuilding Strength

Once range of motion is restored and swelling is controlled, the focus shifts to regaining quad and hamstring strength. Closed-chain exercises — squats, leg press, step-ups — form the backbone of this phase. We use VALD Force Decks to objectively measure limb symmetry, targeting a Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) above 70% before progressing.
Phase 3 — Months 3–6: Neuromuscular Control

Strength alone isn't enough to return safely to sport. This phase introduces progressive plyometrics, agility drills, and sport-specific movement patterns. Balance and proprioception training is critical — the graft is strong enough to tolerate load, but the nervous system needs retraining to protect the joint in dynamic situations.
Phase 4 — Months 6–9: Return-to-Sport Testing

Return to sport is earned through objective testing, not time alone. Our battery includes single-leg hop tests, quad and hamstring strength assessment (LSI >90%), and psychological readiness scoring. Athletes who pass all criteria demonstrate a significantly lower re-injury rate than those cleared on time alone.
Research shows athletes who reach an LSI of 90% or above before returning to sport have a re-rupture risk roughly 4× lower than those who return at 70%.

title: Running Gait Analysis: What It Is and Why Every Runner Needs It
summary: You don't need to be an elite runner to benefit from gait analysis. Understanding how you move is the most direct route to faster times, fewer injuries, and more enjoyable miles.

sections.content: Running looks simple — one foot in front of the other. But the mechanics of how your foot strikes the ground, how your hip extends, and how your trunk stays stable all interact in ways that either protect or stress your joints. Gait analysis brings those interactions into view.
What Does a Gait Assessment Measure?

At Stance, we use a dual wearable sensor system that attaches to your shoes and captures over 25 metrics per step. Key parameters include ground contact time, foot strike pattern, pronation excursion and velocity, braking G-force, and step rate (cadence). These metrics paint a detailed picture of where your body is absorbing excess load.
Common Patterns We Find

items: Overstriding — landing too far ahead of the centre of mass, increasing braking force and knee stress
Excessive pronation — medial collapse at the ankle that often contributes to plantar fasciitis and tibial stress reactions
Reduced cadence — slower step rates correlate with longer ground contact and higher impact loads
Hip drop — insufficient glute medius activation causing lateral knee and IT band stress
Trunk lean — excessive forward or lateral lean indicating core or hip weakness

sections.content: How Findings Translate to Training Changes

A gait report without a corrective plan is just data. Our physios translate each finding into specific cues, drills, and strength targets. A runner with a low cadence might start with a simple metronome cue to increase step rate by 5–10%, which research shows can reduce knee loading by up to 20%.
Even a small cadence increase of 5–8% can meaningfully reduce patellofemoral stress — one of the most common running injury sites.
Who Should Get a Gait Analysis?

Any runner with a recurring injury, anyone preparing for a half or full marathon, and any runner who simply wants to move more efficiently. You don't need to be symptomatic — prevention is always more efficient than treatment.

title: Knee Pain Is Not Just a Running Problem — Here's What's Actually Causing Yours
summary: Most people assume knee pain means the knee is the problem. More often, it's a symptom of dysfunction elsewhere. Understanding the real source changes everything about how you treat it.

sections.content: Knee pain is one of the most common complaints we see at Stance — and one of the most commonly mismanaged. Rest and anti-inflammatories may quiet the pain temporarily, but if the underlying driver isn't addressed, the pain returns. Often stronger.
The Knee Is a Hinge Caught Between Two Joints

The knee has relatively limited mobility — it bends and extends. What it doesn't do well is tolerate rotational or valgus (inward collapse) stress. Those forces typically come from above (stiff hip, weak glutes) or below (limited ankle dorsiflexion, overpronation). When either end is dysfunctional, the knee bears the cost.
Hip Weakness and Knee Pain

Weak hip abductors — glute medius in particular — allow the femur to internally rotate and adduct during single-leg loading. This creates a valgus moment at the knee, compressing the lateral structures and overloading the patellofemoral joint. Strengthening the hip often resolves anterior knee pain without touching the knee itself.
If your knee tracks inward when you squat or descend stairs, that's a classic hip abductor weakness pattern — not a knee alignment problem.
Ankle Stiffness and Knee Pain

When the ankle can't dorsiflex enough (less than 10–15° during weight-bearing), the body compensates by collapsing the foot arch and rotating the tibia inward — both of which translate stress to the knee. Assessing ankle mobility is a standard part of any knee examination at Stance.
What We Do Differently

Rather than treating the knee in isolation, our assessment maps the whole kinetic chain. We screen hip strength, ankle mobility, foot mechanics, and movement quality under load. Treatment follows the findings — which means addressing the root cause, not just the loudest symptom.

title: Why Strength Training Is Non-Negotiable for Runners
summary: The evidence is unambiguous: runners who strength train get injured less and run faster. Yet most recreational runners skip it entirely. Here's the case for making it a permanent part of your training week.

sections.content: Mention strength training to a recreational runner and you'll often hear: 'I don't want to get bulky' or 'I'd rather just run more.' Both reactions are understandable — but both are based on misconceptions. Strength training for runners isn't bodybuilding. It's injury-proofing and performance enhancement.
The Injury-Prevention Evidence

A 2018 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that strength training reduced sports injuries by roughly 50% and overuse injuries specifically by up to two-thirds. For runners — a population with annual injury rates between 40–80% — those numbers are transformative. The mechanism is straightforward: stronger tendons, bones, and muscles tolerate the repetitive loads of running without accumulating the microdamage that leads to stress fractures, shin splints, and tendinopathies.
The Performance Mechanism

Running economy — how efficiently you convert energy into forward motion — is the best predictor of performance beyond VO₂max. Heavy resistance training improves running economy by increasing musculotendinous stiffness, which allows more elastic energy to be stored and returned with each stride. A stiffer Achilles complex means a more efficient toe-off.
Heavy strength training (not high-rep circuits) is what improves running economy. Think 3–5 sets of 4–6 reps at high loads, not 3×20 bodyweight squats.
What to Focus On

items: Single-leg squat and its variations — develops hip stability and quad strength simultaneously
Romanian deadlift — builds posterior chain strength critical for propulsion
Calf raises (heavy, single leg) — directly loads the Achilles and soleus
Nordic hamstring curls — the highest-evidence exercise for hamstring injury prevention
Hip thrust — strengthens glutes through extension, directly translating to running power

sections.content: How Much Is Enough?

Two sessions per week of 30–45 minutes is sufficient to see meaningful injury prevention and performance benefits. The key is consistency over months, not intensity in the short term. Integrate sessions on easy or rest days to avoid compromising quality run sessions.

title: Chronic Back Pain: Why You Keep Getting Better and Then Worse Again
summary: The cycle of improvement and relapse is the hallmark of poorly managed back pain. Breaking that cycle requires understanding what's actually perpetuating it — not just what's triggering it.

sections.content: If you've had back pain that resolved with rest or treatment and then came back months later — often triggered by something minor — you're not alone, and your spine isn't 'falling apart.' What you're experiencing is a very common pattern driven by incomplete rehabilitation.
Why Rest Alone Isn't a Treatment

Rest reduces the mechanical load that's producing pain, which makes you feel better. But it doesn't address the underlying drivers — movement dysfunction, muscle weakness, load tolerance deficits — that made the pain develop in the first place. Once you return to normal activity, those drivers are still present, and the pain returns.
The Three Common Drivers We Find

items: Anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar hyperlordosis — often driven by tight hip flexors and weak deep abdominals
Thoracic stiffness — when the upper back can't rotate, the lumbar spine compensates
Poor load transfer — the deep stabilisers (multifidus, transversus abdominis) not activating before superficial movers

sections.content: Pain location is rarely the problem location in the spine. Where it hurts is where the load is accumulating — not necessarily where the movement restriction originates.
Why Passive Treatment Has Limits

Manual therapy, massage, and spinal manipulation can provide significant short-term relief by modulating pain and improving movement. But evidence consistently shows that active rehabilitation — graded loading, motor control training, progressive strengthening — produces more durable outcomes. Passive treatment is the entry point, not the destination.
Building Durable Capacity

The goal of back pain rehabilitation at Stance isn't to get you pain-free — it's to build a spine robust enough that pain doesn't keep coming back. That means progressive loading beyond the level that previously caused pain, restoring movement variability, and developing the strength to sustain the postures and activities that matter most to you.

title: Return to Sport After Injury: Why the Clock Is the Wrong Metric
summary: "Six weeks and you're good to go" is one of the most dangerous phrases in sports medicine. Time is a proxy for healing, not a guarantee of readiness. Here's what objective return-to-sport criteria actually look like.

sections.content: When someone asks 'how long until I can play again?', the honest answer is 'we don't know yet — it depends on how you respond to rehab and whether you can meet objective criteria.' That's not the reassuring answer athletes want, but it's the only accurate one.
The Problem With Time-Based Clearance

Healing timelines are population averages. Individual variation is enormous, driven by age, fitness, nutrition, sleep, stress, and the specific injury pattern. Two athletes with the same ACL reconstruction may differ by 3–4 months in their actual readiness. Clearing both at 9 months because 'that's the protocol' will over-protect one and under-protect the other.
What Objective Criteria Look Like
At Stance, return-to-sport clearance for lower limb injuries involves a structured test battery across three domains:

items: Strength criteria — Limb Symmetry Index ≥90% for quad and hamstring peak torque, tested with VALD Dynamo
Functional hop tests — single-leg hop, triple hop, crossover hop, and 6-metre timed hop, all ≥90% LSI
Movement quality — video-based movement screening assessing landing mechanics, trunk control, and joint alignment under fatigue
Psychological readiness — validated questionnaires assessing fear of re-injury and confidence in the joint

sections.content: Psychological readiness is often the last criterion to be met — and the most commonly overlooked. Fear of re-injury significantly increases actual re-injury risk.
The Role of Progressive Exposure

Return to sport isn't a binary event — it's a continuum. We structure it in phases: return to training (full team sessions without contact), return to competition (non-contact phases of matches), and unrestricted return (full contact, full competitive load). Each phase has its own criteria and monitoring checkpoints.
What This Means for You

If you've been injured, push your team to give you objective targets, not just a date. Ask: 'What do I need to demonstrate to be cleared?' The answer should be specific numbers and movement standards — not 'you should feel ready by then.'
